opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think coding is one of the most underrated stories in AI, and not only because it makes software engineers more productive, although it clearly does.

The first reason is that code is the cleanest training signal we have. In most domains it's hard to tell whether a model's output is good. With code you can run it. It compiles or it doesn't, the tests pass or they fail. That gives you a natural reward function, so coding is where reinforcement learning and self-improvement loops can really take off. You can generate a program, execute it, look at the result, fix it, and repeat, at huge scale and without a human in the loop for every step. Very few domains give you that.

The second reason is closer to my own work. I think of code as an action space. Years ago, with Voyager in Minecraft, the key insight was that instead of having the agent output low-level keyboard and mouse actions, we let it write code. The code became its skill library. It could store skills, compose them, and build more complex behaviors on top of simpler ones, the way a programmer builds on libraries. That turned out to be a very powerful way to get open-ended, lifelong learning. So when coding models get better, every agent that uses code as its interface gets better too: web agents, game agents, and eventually robots.

That leads to the third reason, which is the long-term one for me. The physical world is the next frontier. In robotics we're bottlenecked on data and on simulation. Coding models can help write simulation environments, generate tasks, design reward functions, and even write the policies themselves. We've already seen early versions of this, where a language model writes reward functions that beat ones designed by human experts. Over 10 years I expect coding models to become something like the meta-tool that builds the training grounds for embodied AI.

So my view is that code is the bridge. It connects language intelligence to action, in the digital world first and then in the physical one. If you think of the model as the brain, code is how it reaches out and actually does things. That's why I think coding models over the next decade will matter well beyond software engineering. They'll shape how we build general-purpose agents.

r001.rationale: The response describes code as a training signal and an action space, but does not characterize coding as a fundamental reasoning task.

r002.rationale: It predicts coding models will shape general-purpose agents over the next decade, but does not suggest they will match human software engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The reason I get so animated about coding models is that code is the one domain where the whole loop closes. You can write a program, run it, see whether it works, and feed that signal straight back into the model. There's no human in the loop grading an essay, no fuzzy judgment about whether a poem is good. The compiler and the unit tests are the reward function, and they're infinitely patient and infinitely scalable.

That matters because it means coding is the first place where models can genuinely self-improve. Once a model can write code, it can write the tools that make the next model better: data pipelines, simulators, evaluation harnesses, even pieces of its own training stack. Coding isn't just one capability among many. It's the capability that bootstraps all the others.

And then there's the robotics angle, which is where I spend most of my time. A robot's policy is ultimately code, or something code-adjacent. If a model can read a task description and synthesize a controller, or write the reward function for a reinforcement learning run, or generate the simulation environment to train in, then the bottleneck on embodied intelligence shifts from scarce human engineering hours to compute. We've already seen early versions of this, where a language model writes the reward shaping that would have taken a grad student weeks, and it beats the human-written version.

So over ten years, I think coding models go from "autocomplete for software engineers" to the substrate that every other kind of AI gets built on. The software engineer of 2036 is going to look a lot more like a director than a typist, and the physical world is going to get the same treatment. That's a pretty exciting arc to be living through.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a self-improvement loop and a foundation for building other AI capabilities, but does not characterize it as a fundamental reasoning task.

r002.rationale: It predicts coding models will reshape software engineering by 2036, with engineers acting more like directors, but does not suggest coding agents will match human engineers within roughly ten years.

astra-6.text:
I’m excited because code is more than a way to build software. It’s a way for an AI to take an idea and make something happen. A model can write a program, run it, see where it fails, and try again. That feedback loop is incredibly powerful: you can test whether something works instead of just judging whether the answer sounds convincing.

Over the next ten years, I think the interesting shift is from models that help you write individual functions to systems that can carry out entire projects with you. You describe what you want, and the model helps work through the design, implementation, testing, and iteration. The hard part is maintaining coherence over a long task and knowing whether you’ve actually solved the right problem.

And coding connects to much more than software engineering. If an AI can write code, it can build tools, analyze experimental results, and interact with simulations. That makes coding a foundation for systems that can learn and do research. That’s what excites me most—the possibility that better coding models help us discover things we didn’t already know how to build.

r001.rationale: The response presents coding as a way for AI to act, test results, and support learning and research, but does not characterize coding as a fundamental reasoning task.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that coding agents may match human software engineers within roughly ten years.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that code gives AI a way to act. A model can describe an idea, but if it can write and run code, it can build something, test it, look at what went wrong, and try again. That feedback loop is incredibly powerful.

And you can often check whether it succeeded. Does the program run? Do the tests pass? Does the result satisfy the constraints? Those checks aren’t perfect, but they give us a concrete signal for improving the model.

Over the next 10 years, I’m excited to see that expand beyond helping you finish a function. You could describe a scientific experiment or a simulation, and the model could help build the tools to explore it. The interesting question becomes: how much of the distance between an idea and a working system can we remove? I think coding models can remove a tremendous amount.

r001.rationale: The response describes code as a way for AI to act, test results, and improve, but does not characterize coding as a fundamental reasoning task.

r002.rationale: It predicts coding models will remove much of the distance between an idea and a working system, but does not suggest they may match human software engineers within roughly ten years.
